title: The Model Was Right. The Harness Failed. — Vinoth Govindarajan, OpenAI

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The talk is about infrastructure patterns and mental models that agent builders use to construct reliable production systems. The harness blueprint, run receipt audit, and five failure shapes are developer-facing architectural guidance for building agent platforms.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The speaker explicitly states the harness blueprint applies to all agent types and presents the five failure shapes as universal patterns, not specific to any vertical or application domain.

summary:
Vinoth Govindarajan, a Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI working on core data infrastructure, presents a talk at QCon AI Boston 2026 titled "The Agent Harness: Control Planes, Invariants, and Approval Boundaries for Production AI Agents." The central thesis is that most production agent failures are harness failures, not model failures — the model is coherent but coherent over a broken history. He opens with a production incident where a user saw a successful reply but the system forgot it happened: delivery succeeded while persistence failed, leaving the next turn to sound coherent over broken state. Silent success, he argues, is worse than a crash because it gives a lie.

The talk introduces a production contract: the model proposes, the harness commits, and the receipt proves it. The model is never the production boundary; the harness owns state transitions, authority checks, ordered commits, and evidence. Three takeaways frame the talk: own the state, order the mutation, prove the action. A fact needs one owner and one replay path; shared mutable state needs one ordered commit path; a transcript is not proof.

The harness blueprint describes how events enter from many surfaces, a control plane maps them to a session key, a session lane gives one active writer, the runtime calls models and tools, tools act through approvals and policies, and the audit trail becomes the run receipt. The runtime is stateless — the harness rebuilds working state each turn. Coherence does not prove completeness.

Five failure shapes are examined using OpenClaw (an open-source personal AI assistant framework) as the case study: (1) State hole — a Telegram reply succeeded but the turn was never persisted; (2) Overlapping writers — two callers load-modify-save the same state and the second save silently erases the first; (3) Dangling tool call — a session contains a tool call with no matching result, blocking all subsequent messages; (4) Approval drift — an expired approval was treated as retriable, surviving restarts and blocking later work; (5) Missing edge proof — a message tool reported success but the message never rendered. Each failure represents a missing boundary around state ownership, ordering, time, authority, or user-visible proof.

The talk closes with the run receipt audit: five questions — what woke it up (trigger identity), what state did it inherit (working set), what authority did it use (bound to one pending action), what executed (side-effect boundary records), and what evidence survived (user-visible proof). Applying the audit to the opening incident reveals that delivery survived while state did not — that gap is the harness failure. The agent did not need a better model or prompt; the system needed a better harness with a complete receipt. Once text can become an action, the question shifts from whether the model can reason to whether the system can own state, order mutations, bound work, constrain authority, and preserve evidence. Resources mentioned: the OpenAI Agents SDK and The Agent Stack newsletter.
whyItMatters: The software engineering concepts and AI concepts in this talk form a unified framework for production agent reliability. The production contract (propose-commit-prove) is the organizing principle: it separates model reasoning from system integrity and assigns clear responsibilities to each layer. The five failure shapes are each a missing boundary in this contract — state ownership, ordering, time, authority, and evidence — and they draw on both traditional distributed systems patterns (single writer lanes, ordered commit paths, idempotency, deadlines) and AI-specific concerns (tool call lifecycles, model requestability vs authority, coherent-over-broken-state). The run receipt audit synthesizes these concepts into a diagnostic tool that asks five questions mapping directly to the five boundaries. What makes these concepts matter together is that they reframe the evaluation of agent systems: instead of asking whether the model can reason, the framework asks whether the system can own state, order mutations, bound work, constrain authority, and preserve evidence. The OpenClaw case study grounds each concept in a real production incident, demonstrating that these are not theoretical concerns but recurring failure modes in deployed agent systems.
temporalContext: The talk was presented at QCon AI Boston 2026 on June 2, 2026, and the YouTube video was published on 2026-07-29. Research was conducted as of 2026-08-23. The OpenAI Agents SDK Python repo was created 2025-03-11 and the JS repo on 2025-05-31. OpenClaw was created on 2025-11-24 and had moved to the OpenClaw Foundation nonprofit structure by February 2026. The talk reflects the state of production agent architecture thinking in mid-2026, when agent harness reliability was an active concern as deployments scaled.

Own the state, order the mutation, prove the action. One fact needs one owner and one replay path; shared mutable state needs one ordered commit path.
A transcript records what the agent said; a receipt records what the system allowed, attempted, executed, and what the user-visible edge confirmed.
Silent success is worse than a crash—it gives a lie. Delivery succeeding while persistence fails leaves no alarm.
Five failure shapes to look for: state holes, overlapping writers, dangling tool calls, approval drift, and missing edge proof.
Approval is a scoped execution state, not a vague memory—bound to the action with actor, session, tool, arguments, scope, and lifetime.

concepts.name: Harness failure vs model failure
concepts.explanation: The distinction between failures caused by the model's reasoning and failures caused by the surrounding system (harness) that manages state, ordering, authority, and evidence. Most production agent failures are harness failures — the model is coherent but coherent over a broken history.
concepts.importance: This is the central thesis of the talk and reframes how practitioners should evaluate agent reliability: from model reasoning quality to system integrity.

concepts.name: Agent harness blueprint (control plane, session lanes, runtime, audit trail)
concepts.explanation: A universal architecture for agent systems: events enter from many surfaces, a control plane maps them to a session key, a session lane gives one active writer, the runtime calls models and tools, tools act through approvals and policies, and the audit trail becomes the run receipt. The speaker presents this as applicable to all agent types.
concepts.importance: Provides the architectural mental model within which all five failure shapes and the run receipt audit are situated.

concepts.name: Tool call lifecycle and dangling tool calls
concepts.explanation: A tool call in an agent session must have a matching tool result. A dangling tool call — one with no matching result — blocks all subsequent messages because the agent runtime waits for an event that will never arrive. Silence is not a terminal state. This is specific to the tool-calling mechanism of LLM agents.
concepts.importance: The third failure shape is unique to agent architectures that use tool calling; it has no direct analogue in traditional request-response systems.

concepts.name: Approval as scoped execution state in agent systems
concepts.explanation: In agent systems where the model can request actions, approval must be a scoped execution state bound to the specific action: who approved, in what session and run, which tool, which arguments, what scope, what lifetime. This is distinct from traditional access control because the model's requestability is not authority. Approval drift occurs when expired approvals persist across restarts.
concepts.importance: The fourth failure shape; unique to agent systems where a model intermediary can request actions on behalf of users, requiring dynamic authority scoping.

concepts.name: User-visible edge proof for agent actions
concepts.explanation: A tool reporting success internally does not prove the user saw the result. In agent systems that send messages or perform external actions, proof is a chain: model proposed, policy allowed or denied, execution attempted, user-visible edge confirmed. The receipt preserves the chain. This is specific to agent systems where the model can trigger user-facing side effects.
concepts.importance: The fifth failure shape; addresses the gap between internal tool success and external user-visible confirmation, a problem that arises when LLM agents are given tools that interact with users.

concepts.name: Context rehydration and coherent-over-broken-state
concepts.explanation: The agent runtime is stateless — the harness rebuilds working state each turn. When state is incomplete or corrupted, the model still produces coherent output over that broken context. Coherence does not prove completeness. This is a failure mode unique to LLM-based agents that can sound correct even when their context is missing critical facts.
concepts.importance: Explains why harness failures are insidious: the model's coherence masks the underlying state corruption, making failures silent and hard to detect.

concepts.name: Least privilege for agent tool surfaces
concepts.explanation: Capability is not execution; the model can request an action, but requestability is not authority. Least privilege narrows the tool surface available to the model. This applies the security principle of least privilege specifically to the agent tool-calling context, where the model's ability to call a tool does not mean it is authorized to execute that action.
concepts.importance: Connects security governance to agent architecture; the tool surface exposed to the model must be narrowed to what the session and action context authorize.

concepts.name: Production contract (propose-commit-prove)
concepts.explanation: A three-part contract where the model proposes an action, the harness commits the state transition, and the receipt proves what was allowed, attempted, executed, and confirmed at the user-visible edge. The model is never the production boundary.
concepts.importance: This is the foundational principle of the talk — all five failure shapes and the run receipt audit derive from this contract.

concepts.name: State ownership and system of record
concepts.explanation: Every fact needs one owner — the component that can reconstruct reality. Storage tells where bytes live; ownership tells who can replay the fact. The state hole failure shape is a missing ownership boundary where delivery succeeded but the turn was never persisted to the system of record.
concepts.importance: The first of the five failure shapes; without clear state ownership, silent success can occur where delivery succeeds while persistence fails.

concepts.name: Single writer lane and ordered commit path
concepts.explanation: One ordered commit path per mutable state boundary. Commits must be serialized via queue, mutex, transaction, or lock, scoped conservatively to commit time. Concurrency is fine for reads and independent retrieval. Two correct writes can still produce one wrong outcome because last-writer-wins is not a consistency model.
concepts.importance: The second failure shape (overlapping writers) is a direct consequence of missing this boundary; it causes silent data loss that looks like success.

concepts.name: Deadlines, cancellation, and terminal states for external boundaries
concepts.explanation: Every external boundary needs an ending: success, failure, timeout, cancel, or max attempts. Silence is not a terminal state. A dangling tool call with no matching result blocks all subsequent messages behind an event that will never arrive. Runs need watchdogs, tool error results, and recovery channels that do not wait behind stuck work.
concepts.importance: The third failure shape (dangling tool call) directly results from missing time and cancellation boundaries; it causes indefinite blocking of agent runs.

concepts.name: Scoped execution state for approval and authority
concepts.explanation: Approval must be a scoped execution state bound to the action: who approved, in what session and run, which tool, which arguments, what scope, what lifetime, and what outcome. Capability is not execution; requestability is not authority. Least privilege narrows the tool surface. An expired approval treated as retriable that survives restarts is approval drift.
concepts.importance: The fourth failure shape (approval drift) is a direct consequence of missing bounded authority; it allows expired approvals to persist and block work.

concepts.name: Side-effect boundary records vs internal success
concepts.explanation: Internal success is not external proof. A tool reporting success internally does not prove the user saw the result. Proof is a chain: model proposed, policy allowed or denied, execution attempted, user-visible edge confirmed. Execution records must capture actual side effects, not agent intentions. The receipt preserves the chain.
concepts.importance: The fifth failure shape (missing edge proof) results from conflating internal success with user-visible proof; without side-effect boundary records, the system cannot verify delivery.

concepts.name: Run receipt audit
concepts.explanation: A five-question diagnostic for production agent incidents: (1) What woke it up — trigger identity for deduplication, order, and authorization; (2) What state did it inherit — transcript, session state, memory snapshot, policy version, tool surface; (3) What authority did it use — bound to one pending action with actor, session, tool, arguments, scope, lifetime; (4) What executed — tool/API call, arguments, attempt number, idempotency key, external results as a side-effect boundary; (5) What evidence survived — at the boundary the user cares about.
concepts.importance: This is the closing diagnostic tool of the talk, applied to the opening incident to reveal that the broken boundary was state ownership, not model reasoning.

concepts.name: Stateless agent runtime with context rehydration
concepts.explanation: The runtime is stateless — the harness rebuilds working state each turn from the system of record. Coherence over the rebuilt context does not prove completeness of the underlying state. This pattern means that missing or corrupted state is silently carried forward.
concepts.importance: Explains why coherent model output over broken state is the signature failure mode; the model cannot detect that the context it was given is incomplete.

concepts.name: Idempotency keys and bounded retry
concepts.explanation: Execution records include attempt number and idempotency key as part of the side-effect boundary. External boundaries need max attempts. Approval is scoped with a lifetime. These mechanisms ensure that retries do not produce duplicate side effects and that work is bounded before it bounds the system.
concepts.importance: Supports the deadlines and cancellation failure shape and the scoped approval pattern; without idempotency and bounded retry, the system cannot safely recover from failures.

sections.title: Introduction: harness failures vs model failures
sections.summary: The speaker opens by arguing most agent failures are harness failures, not model failures. A production incident is introduced: the user saw a reply, the system forgot it happened. The user-visible edge looked healthy while the durable record had a hole.

sections.title: Delivery can succeed while the truth fails
sections.summary: The incident is detailed: an agent was asked to remember a refund, said it recorded it, but the next turn could not recall it. Silent success gives a lie—delivery succeeds while persistence fails, and the next turn sounds coherent over broken history. A crash at least gives a boundary.

sections.title: A model proposes, the harness commits, the receipt proves
sections.summary: Speaker introduces himself from OpenAI core data and AI infrastructure. Presents the production contract: model proposes, harness commits, receipt proves. Three takeaways: own the state, order the mutation, prove the action. Transcript is not proof; a receipt records what was allowed, attempted, executed, and confirmed at the user-visible edge.

sections.title: How events enter and state is rehydrated
sections.summary: The harness blueprint: events enter from many surfaces, control plane maps them to a session key, session lane gives one active writer, runtime calls models and tools, tools act through approvals and policies, audit trail becomes the run receipt. The runtime is stateless—harness rebuilds working state each turn. Coherence does not prove completeness.

sections.title: Ownership: who persists the turn
sections.summary: First failure shape: state hole. OpenClaw Telegram reply succeeded but the turn was not written to the transcript. The missing boundary was state ownership—who is the system of record that can replay the fact? Storage tells where bytes live; ownership tells who can reconstruct reality.

sections.title: Single writer lanes and overlapping writes
sections.summary: Second failure shape: overlapping writers. Two callers load the same old state, each changes a different record, second save silently erases the first. Rule: one ordered commit path for one mutable state boundary. Concurrency is fine for reads and independent retrieval; commits must be serialized via queue, mutex, transaction, or lock, scoped conservatively to commit time.

sections.title: Time, deadlines, and cancellation
sections.summary: Third failure shape: dangling tool call. A session contains a tool call with no matching result; the run waits for an event that will never arrive. Runs need deadlines, cancellation, watchdogs, tool error results, and recovery channels that do not wait behind stuck work. Every external boundary needs an ending.

sections.title: Approval drift and bounded authority
sections.summary: Fourth failure shape: approval drift. An expired approved callback was treated as retriable, surviving restarts and blocking later work. Approval must be a scoped execution state bound to the action: who approved, in what session and run, which tool, which arguments, how long, what outcome, and pointing to the receipt. Capability is not execution; least privilege narrows the tool surface.

sections.title: Internal success vs user-visible proof
sections.summary: Fifth failure shape: missing edge proof. A message tool reported success but the message never rendered. Internal success is not external proof. Proof is a chain: model proposed, policy allowed/denied, execution attempted, user-visible edge confirmed. The receipt preserves the chain.

sections.title: The run receipt audit: five questions and application
sections.summary: Each audit question is expanded with specifics: trigger identity for deduplication, order, and authorization; inherited working set—transcript, session state, memory snapshot, policy version, tool surface; authority bound to one pending action with actor, session, tool, run, arguments, scope, lifetime; execution record—tool/API call, arguments, attempt number, idempotency key, external results as a side-effect boundary; evidence at the boundary the user cares about. Applied to the opening incident: trigger was a user message, broken boundary was state ownership, execution was the channel send, and the gap between delivery surviving and state not surviving is the harness failure. The agent did not need a better model or prompt; the system needed a better harness with a complete receipt. Once text becomes action, ask whether the system can own state, order mutations, bound work, constrain authority, and preserve evidence. Resources: OpenAI Agents SDK and The Agent Stack newsletter.

demonstrations: OpenClaw Telegram reply issue: a reply succeeded at the user-visible edge but the router turn was never written to the active context or transcript, leaving the next turn with no durable record.
OpenClaw overlapping writer issue: two callers loaded the same old state, each changed a different record, and the second save silently erased the first.
OpenClaw dangling tool call issue: a session contained a tool call with no matching tool result, blocking all subsequent messages behind a silence that would never resolve.
OpenClaw approval drift issue: an expired approved callback was treated as retriable, persisted across restarts, and blocked later channel work.
OpenClaw missing edge proof issue: a message tool reported success for a web chat or TUI run, but the message did not render—internal success did not equal user-visible proof.

Run receipt audit applied to the opening incident: trigger was a user message, the broken boundary was state ownership, execution was the channel send, and the gap between delivery surviving and state not surviving is the harness failure.
limitations: Talk uses OpenClaw as a single public case study; the speaker notes it is not an OpenClaw product pitch.
The harness blueprint is presented as universal across agent types but is a mental model, not an empirical survey.
Resources referenced are the OpenAI Agents SDK and The Agent Stack newsletter for further exploration.
quantitativeClaims: The run receipt audit has five questions per incident.
Five failure shapes to look for: state holes, overlapping writers, dangling tool calls, approval drift, missing edge proof.
Three things to remember from the talk: own the state, order the mutation, prove the action.

organization.name: OpenAI

technologies.label: Agent Harness Architecture
technologies.summary: The agent harness architecture is the production system boundary around the LLM model. It owns state transitions, authority checks, ordered commits, and evidence preservation. The talk presents a production contract where the model proposes, the harness commits, and the receipt proves what happened. The harness blueprint includes a control plane mapping events to session keys, single-writer session lanes, a stateless runtime that rehydrates working state each turn, tools acting through approvals and policies, and an audit trail that becomes the run receipt. Five failure shapes—state holes, overlapping writers, dangling tool calls, approval drift, and missing edge proof—illustrate what happens when boundaries in this architecture are missing. The harness is distinct from the model: it is the system of record for state, the enforcer of ordering and authority, and the preserver of evidence.
technologies.role: This is the central technology of the talk. The speaker presents the harness architecture as a universal pattern applicable to all agent types, using it to frame five production failure shapes and a diagnostic audit. The production contract (model proposes, harness commits, receipt proves) is the organizing principle of the entire talk.

technologies.label: OpenAI Agents SDK
technologies.summary: The OpenAI Agents SDK is an official OpenAI framework for building multi-agent workflows. It provides an agent loop, orchestration and handoffs, guardrails and human review, sessions and resumable run state, tracing and observability, and tools including MCP. These features map directly to the harness blueprint taught in the talk: the agent loop is the runtime, guardrails enforce approval and authority boundaries, sessions provide state ownership and rehydration, and tracing constitutes the audit trail. The speaker explicitly recommends the SDK as a resource at the end of the talk. Both Python and JavaScript/TypeScript implementations are available with MIT licenses.
technologies.role: Explicitly mentioned by the speaker as a resource at the end of the talk for exploring the harness architecture concepts further. The speaker's employer, OpenAI, develops and maintains the SDK.

technologies.label: Run Receipt Audit
technologies.summary: The run receipt audit is a five-question diagnostic technique for production agent incidents: (1) What woke it up—trigger identity for deduplication, ordering, and authorization; (2) What state did it inherit—transcript, session state, memory snapshot, policy version, tool surface; (3) What authority did it use—bound to one pending action with actor, session, tool, arguments, scope, lifetime; (4) What executed—tool/API calls, arguments, attempt number, idempotency key, external results as side-effect boundary records; (5) What evidence survived—at the user-visible edge. The talk applies this audit to the opening incident to reveal that the broken boundary was state ownership, not model reasoning. A transcript records what the agent said; a receipt records what the system allowed, attempted, executed, and what the user-visible edge confirmed.
technologies.role: Closing diagnostic framework of the talk; the speaker applies the five-question audit to the opening production incident to demonstrate that the failure was a harness boundary gap (state ownership), not a model reasoning problem. The audit synthesizes all five failure shapes into a single diagnostic tool.

technologies.label: OpenClaw
technologies.summary: OpenClaw is an open-source, self-hosted personal AI assistant framework created by Peter Steinberger and developed by the OpenClaw Foundation (a nonprofit). It connects AI models to messaging channels including WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Slack, Signal, and iMessage through a Gateway architecture with persistent memory and on-device state. In the talk, OpenClaw serves as the primary case study: five real production incidents illustrate the five failure shapes of harness architecture—the Telegram reply that succeeded but was never persisted (state hole), two callers whose overlapping writes silently erased data (overlapping writers), a tool call with no matching result blocking all messages (dangling tool call), an expired approval treated as retriable surviving restarts (approval drift), and a message tool reporting success without the message rendering (missing edge proof). The speaker notes this is not an OpenClaw product pitch.
technologies.role: Primary case study platform throughout the entire talk. Five real OpenClaw production incidents are used to illustrate each of the five harness failure shapes: the Telegram reply that succeeded but was never persisted (state hole), two callers whose overlapping writes silently erased data (overlapping writers), a tool call with no matching result blocking all messages (dangling tool call), an expired approval surviving restarts (approval drift), and a message tool reporting success without the message rendering (missing edge proof).

outcomes: Distinguish harness failures from model failures and identify five recurring failure shapes in agent systems
Apply the production contract — model proposes, harness commits, receipt proves — to evaluate agent reliability
Run the five-question run receipt audit on a production agent path to expose gaps in state, authority, execution, and evidence
Design state ownership with a single system of record and one ordered commit path per mutable state boundary
Bound external actions with deadlines, cancellation, and scoped approval objects that stay bound to the authorized action
Shift evaluation from model reasoning quality to system integrity across state ownership, ordering, authority, and evidence preservation
challengeSeeds: Given an agent harness with a state hole — delivery succeeds but the turn is not persisted — apply the run receipt audit to identify the broken boundary and implement the fix
Reproduce the overlapping writers failure: two concurrent callers load-modify-save the same session state; implement single-writer serialization and verify no silent data loss
Inject a dangling tool call into a session and implement deadlines, cancellation, and recovery channels so silence is never a terminal state
Create an approval drift scenario where an expired approval survives a restart; redesign approval as a scoped execution state and verify it does not persist beyond its lifetime
Build a tool that reports internal success without user-visible proof; add edge-proof verification and demonstrate the gap between internal success and external confirmation
Implement the full five-question run receipt audit as a diagnostic tool and apply it to a multi-incident agent system to classify each failure shape

evidence.supports: A tool reporting success internally does not prove the user saw the result.

evidence.excerpt: What woke it up? A user message, web hook, timer, tool result, sub agent, or a replay. Name the trigger and its identity. Without that, you cannot reason about dduplication, order, or authorization.
evidence.supports: First audit question requires trigger identity for reasoning about deduplication, ordering, and authorization.

evidence.excerpt: A model request is not permission. Authority should bind to a one pending action.
evidence.supports: Authority must be scoped to a single pending action, not granted broadly.

evidence.excerpt: This is a side effect boundary, not the poor summary of what the agent intended.
evidence.supports: Execution records must capture actual side effects, not agent intentions.

evidence.excerpt: The agent did not need a better model. The model did not need a better prompt. The system needed a better harness with complete receipt.
evidence.supports: The fix for the opening incident was harness completeness, not model or prompt improvement.
